excerpt: Paano magtanim ng sampalok? Here is how traditional Filipino farmers usually plant sampalok (tamarind), step by step from getting the field ready to the harvest, with the day of each step and what to change for a higher yield.

heroImage.alt: Young fruit trees planted in straight rows on cleared red soil

blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant sampalok. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

How Filipino growers plant sampalok, the sour kind for sinigang and candy and the sweet kind eaten fresh, either from seed the old way or from grafted seedlings that bear much sooner. It is a tough, long lived tree for dry corners, field edges, dikes and backyards.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [sampalok nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/tamarind-nutrient-deficiency). For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant sampalok

Trees are planted as the rains begin, about May to June. Grafting and budding are done in the cool dry months, about November to January. Trees flower in the rainy months. Green pods for cooking are picked as they fill, and the ripe brown pods come mostly in the dry months early in the year.
What you plant

Most old trees grew from seed, but seedlings do not come true: the fruit may be sour or sweet, small or big, and the tree takes many years to bear. Seeds from big, well filled pods are washed and soaked in water overnight before sowing. For sweet tamarind or a known sour type, farmers buy cleft grafted or budded seedlings from a nursery.
Paano magtanim ng sampalok: grafted seedlings

This is the grafted seedlings way (Grafted seedlings (punla na grafted)). Grafted trees usually start bearing in three to four years, some as early as two. We count the first harvest at 48 months (1,440 days). The crop is ready about 4 years after planting.
Grafted seedlings: before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 30 days before planting: Dig the holes far apart
items.text: Pick a sunny spot where water drains, and dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep about 8 to 10 m apart. Mix the topsoil with rotted manure or compost and fill it back.

blocks.text: Grafted seedlings: planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant at the start of the rains
items.text: On a cloudy day, water the bag, cut it off, and set the seedling at the same depth it grew with the graft joint above the soil. Firm the soil, water, and tie the plant to a stake.

blocks.text: Grafted seedlings: care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 3: Mulch the base
items.text: Spread dry grass or leaves around the seedling, not against the stem, to keep the soil damp.

items.title: Day 30: First feed
items.text: A month after planting, scatter about 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) in a ring away from the stem, and give the same again as the rains end. Manure or compost works too.

items.title: Month 2: Remove shoots below the graft
items.text: Rub off any shoot that grows from the rootstock below the graft joint, and weed a ring under the tree every month or two.

items.title: Month 5: Water through the first dry season
items.text: Water once or twice a week when the rains stop, until the young tree has passed its first dry season. Older trees need no watering.

items.title: Month 12: Shape a low, open tree
items.text: Cut the tip to make it branch and keep three or four well spaced main branches. Remove low, crossing and crowded branches so light gets in and the pods are easy to reach.

items.title: Month 40: Watch the pods for borers
items.text: Once the tree flowers and sets pods, look for holes and frass on the pods from borers and weevils, and pick up and bury fallen damaged pods.

blocks.text: Grafted seedlings: harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 4: Pick the pods
items.text: Grafted trees bear at about three to four years. Pick green, firm pods for sinigang as they fill. For ripe sampalok, wait until the shell turns brown, brittle and loose and the pulp turns sticky and brown, then clip the bunches so the pods do not crack. Tip: Sweet types are also picked half ripe, when the skin peels easily and the pulp is still crisp.

items.title: Month 49: Dry and store the ripe pods
items.text: Spread ripe pods in the sun on mats for a few days, then keep them in clean sacks or jars in a dry place. Pulp for candy is peeled and seeded by hand.

items.title: Month 50: Prune and feed after harvest
items.text: After the ripe pods are in, cut out dead, crowded and crossing branches, and give manure plus about 500 g of ammonium sulfate or complete fertilizer twice a year, more as the tree grows.

blocks.text: From seed, step by step

This is the from seed way (From seed (punla mula sa buto)). Seedling trees stay young and fruitless for five years or longer. We count the first harvest at 72 months (2,160 days). The crop is ready about 6 years after planting.
From seed: before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 30 days before planting: Dig the holes
items.text: Dig holes about 50 cm wide and deep in a sunny, well drained place, far from houses, and mix the topsoil with manure.

blocks.text: From seed: the nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 8 months before planting: Soak and sow the seeds
items.text: Wash the seeds of big, well filled pods and soak them in water overnight. Sow them about 2 cm deep in bags of garden soil and compost and keep them moist. They come up in one to two weeks.

items.title: 7 months before planting: Keep one strong seedling
items.text: Leave the strongest seedling in each bag and keep the bags weeded and watered.

blocks.text: From seed: planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant at the start of the rains
items.text: Set out seedlings that have grown in the bag for up to a year, at the same depth. Firm the soil, water and mulch.

blocks.text: From seed: care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 30: Feed and weed
items.text: Give a small amount of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) or manure a month after planting and at the end of the rains, and keep a clean ring under the tree.

items.title: Month 12: Shape the young tree
items.text: Cut the tip to make it branch and keep three or four main branches.

blocks.text: From seed: harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 6: Pick the first pods
items.text: Seedling trees bear from about five years, often later. Taste the first pods. A tree with poor fruit can be top worked with grafts of a good sweet or sour type.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for sampalok
Spacing

Grafted trees about 8 to 10 m apart each way, about 100 to 150 trees a hectare. Seedling trees grow bigger and are planted farther apart, or alone along dikes, roads and boundaries. One seedling a hole.
Water
Rain fed. Young trees are watered once or twice a week in their first dry season. After that sampalok stands long droughts and bears with no watering at all.
Fertilizer

Rotted manure and compost at planting. Farmers who buy fertilizer give about 100 to 200 g of ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) a tree a month after planting and again at the end of the rains, then about 500 g twice a year once bearing, up to 2 kg a year on a big tree. Many trees get nothing and still bear. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Ring weeding and mulch while young, watering only in the first dry season, shaping the tree to three or four main branches, removing rootstock shoots on grafted trees, and pruning after the harvest. Fallen, bored pods are gathered and buried.
When and how to harvest

Green pods are picked for sinigang as soon as they fill. Ripe pods are picked when the shell is brown, brittle and loose and the pulp sticky. Sweet types are also sold half ripe. Bunches are clipped, not shaken down, so the pods do not crack, then sun dried on mats and kept dry in sacks or jars.
Common mistakes when planting sampalok

items: Planting seed from unknown pods and waiting many years for small or poor fruit.
Planting too close to houses, wells or other trees.
Shaking or beating the branches to drop pods, which cracks them and breaks the twigs.
Storing ripe pods damp, so they mold and draw weevils.
Never pruning, so the tree grows tall and dense and bears less.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of sampalok
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Plant grafted or budded seedlings of a known sweet or sour type for fruit in three to four years.
Top work old poor trees with grafts of a good type.
Prune after harvest to open the tree. Experienced growers also girdle branches before flowering, but learn it from them first.
Test the soil and feed by the result, twice a year.
Scout for pod borers and weevils, clean up fallen pods, and use integrated pest management.

blocks.text: Questions about planting sampalok

items.a: How Filipino growers plant sampalok, the sour kind for sinigang and candy and the sweet kind eaten fresh, either from seed the old way or from grafted seedlings that bear much sooner. Follow the steps above in order, from getting the field ready to the harvest, then change one thing at a time for a higher yield.

items.q: When do farmers plant sampalok in the Philippines?
items.a: Trees are planted as the rains begin, about May to June. Grafting and budding are done in the cool dry months, about November to January.

items.q: How far apart do you plant sampalok?
items.a: Grafted trees about 8 to 10 m apart each way, about 100 to 150 trees a hectare. Seedling trees grow bigger and are planted farther apart, or alone along dikes, roads and boundaries.

items.q: How long before sampalok can be harvested?
items.a: Grafted seedlings, it is ready about 4 years after planting. From seed, it is ready about 6 years after planting. Green pods are picked for sinigang as soon as they fill.

items.q: What do you plant to grow sampalok?
items.a: Most old trees grew from seed, but seedlings do not come true: the fruit may be sour or sweet, small or big, and the tree takes many years to bear. Seeds from big, well filled pods are washed and soaked in water overnight before sowing.
